ai_assistance: Drafted with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) from the team's cited agronomy package, FAO-56 and K-State sources; the team should check values against those sources. Disclosed per Space Apps AI rules.
notes: Triggers are evaluated by recommend.mjs against the analysis output plus a 'derived' block (see recommend.mjs deriveContext). A missing value never triggers an action.
evidence_level: A = regional field trial / extension research; B = general extension guidance; C = rule of thumb.
No action promises a yield, profit or water saving. Corn, sorghum and wheat are all grasses: no family-break credit (T1_R10).
rotation_candidates copy the agronomy package (research/deliverables/agronomy/agronomy.json, reviewed 2026-11-14) so the deployed dashboard is self-contained.
why_template may be a list: recommend.mjs uses the first one whose placeholders all have values.

actions.title: Check irrigation timing: the root zone is past the stress point
actions.why_template: Estimated root-zone depletion has passed the point where {crop} starts to lose yield (FAO-56 p = {p}) on {stress_days} days this season.

evidence_specs.text: Days past the stress point this season: {value}
First estimated stress day: {value}

benefits: Water applied before and during the most sensitive stages is used where it matters most for yield (K-State limited-irrigation guidance).
risks: The bucket model is simplified (no runoff, no capillary rise) and can be wrong by days.
Extra pumping now uses allocation you may need later in the season.
gaps: Estimated from NASA POWER regional weather (~50 km cell) and SSURGO soil storage, not a measurement in your field.
Your actual irrigation events are only known if you enter them in My farm records.
actions.expert_check: Confirm with a soil probe or K-State KanSched before changing your schedule. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Prioritise limited water around pollination
actions.why_template: Your allocation ({alloc} mm) is below the estimated typical irrigation need ({need} mm), and the {window} window is coming up. K-State research shows reproductive stages are where limited water pays back most.

evidence_specs.text: Annual allocation in your records: {value} mm
Median estimated irrigation need for your rotation: {value} mm
Growing degree days since planting: {value} °C·d

benefits: Concentrates scarce water on tasseling, silking and early grain fill, the stages K-State identifies as most yield-sensitive.
risks: Holding back water early can stress the crop if the early season turns hot and dry.
Well capacity may not allow a large catch-up irrigation later (see the capacity check).
gaps: Estimated from NASA POWER regional weather (~50 km cell) and SSURGO soil storage, not a measurement in your field.
Crop stage is estimated from regional GDD and the hybrid in crops.json, not observed in your field.
actions.expert_check: Plan the schedule with K-State KanSched or the Crop Water Allocator. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Your well may not keep up with peak demand: consider fewer irrigated acres or a lower-peak crop on part of the pivot
why_template: Peak 7-day crop demand (about {peak} mm/day) is higher than what the well can deliver on this field (about {well} mm/day). A season total can look fine while July cannot be met.
In {short} seasons of the weather record, the simulated peak 7-day demand of {rot} was higher than this well can deliver. A season total can look fine while July cannot be met.

evidence_specs.text: {value}
Seasons when simulated peak demand exceeded the well: {value}

benefits: Matching irrigated acres or crop peak to well output avoids spreading water too thin in July.
risks: Splitting a pivot between crops adds management, equipment and marketing work.
Phase-split accounting (two crops on one pivot in the same year) is NOT modelled here: the tool compares whole-field sequences only.
gaps: Well capacity is what you entered; actual output, downtime and efficiency were not measured.
Estimated from NASA POWER regional weather (~50 km cell) and SSURGO soil storage, not a measurement in your field.
actions.expert_check: Have the well output measured and talk to your groundwater district (GMD 4) about how splits are accounted. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Your current rotation runs short of water often: compare corn–sorghum and corn–wheat
actions.why_template: Under a {alloc} mm allocation, {rot} would have run short of water in {short} seasons of the weather record.

evidence_specs.text: Seasons with a shortfall under your allocation: {value}
Median shortfall in those seasons: {value} mm

benefits: Direct western Kansas limited-irrigation trials tested all three sequences; none is a universal winner, so a comparison on your own weather record is the useful step.
risks: Rotations change equipment, marketing and herbicide plans (see the rotation cards).
Shortfall is estimated crop demand minus rain and allocation; it is not metered pumping.
gaps: No yield or profit estimate is given: verified response functions and your costs are missing (agronomy rule T1_R14).
Estimated from NASA POWER regional weather (~50 km cell) and SSURGO soil storage, not a measurement in your field.
actions.expert_check: Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Pollination often meets hot days: consider planting date or hybrid maturity
actions.why_template: {sentence}. Moving silking by a week or two (planting date or hybrid maturity) changes which days it meets.

evidence_specs.text: {value}

benefits: Shifting planting date or hybrid maturity moves silking by days to weeks, which can move it away from the usual hottest stretch.
risks: Earlier planting raises cold-soil and frost risk; later or shorter hybrids can lower yield potential.
Heat cannot be avoided reliably: the hottest week moves from year to year.
gaps: Air temperature is from a ~50 km POWER cell; canopy temperature in an irrigated field is lower.
Silking GDD depends on your hybrid's rating.
actions.expert_check: Check hybrid maturity options with your seed dealer. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Planting falls near the typical last frost: watch the forecast and soil temperature
actions.why_template: Your planned planting ({plant}) is within two weeks of the typical last spring frost ({frost}) for this location.

evidence_specs.text: Typical last spring frost (median, POWER record): {value}
Last spring frost this year: {value}
Planned planting date: {value}

benefits: Waiting for a warm, settling forecast lowers the risk of uneven emergence.
risks: Waiting too long pushes pollination later into the hottest part of July (see T1).
gaps: Frost dates use 2-m air temperature from a ~50 km cell; low spots in the field can be colder.
Soil temperature is not in the data used.
actions.expert_check: Check the Kansas Mesonet soil temperature near you before planting. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Corn to wheat: check that corn harvest leaves time for timely wheat sowing
actions.why_template: Your rotation puts winter wheat right after corn. The northwest Kansas wheat target is around {target}, and corn harvest often runs later; a trial recorded a Sep 29 corn harvest followed by Oct 1 sowing.

evidence_specs.text: Statewide historical corn harvest range: {value}
Northwest Kansas wheat sowing target: around {value}

benefits: Planning the handoff (hybrid maturity, drying, drill availability) keeps the corn–wheat option open.
risks: Late sowing after corn can mean poor establishment; corn residue and volunteer wheat raise wheat streak mosaic and Fusarium concerns (T1_R11).
gaps: Your field-ready date and drill availability are not known to the tool (rule T1_R05).
actions.expert_check: Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Root zone is drier than usual before planting: decide on pre-plant water and keep residue
actions.why_template: Root-zone wetness is at the {pct}th percentile for this date: drier than most years going into the next season.
benefits: Retained residue and no-till reduce evaporation, so more off-season rain stays in the profile.
risks: Pre-plant irrigation uses allocation early, and some is lost to evaporation and drainage before the crop can use it.
gaps: POWER root-zone wetness is model-based (MERRA-2 reanalysis), not a satellite or probe measurement.
Starting profile water in your field is unknown (rule T1_R01).
actions.expert_check: Take a soil probe reading before deciding on pre-plant water. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Long low-green-cover periods: keep residue and no-till to cut evaporation and wind erosion
actions.why_template: Satellite greenness shows about {months} months a year with low green cover on this field. Residue is what protects the soil in those months.

evidence_specs.text: Months per year with low green cover (MODIS NDVI < 0.3): {value}

benefits: Standing and flat residue reduce soil-surface evaporation and wind erosion; the limited-irrigation trials were run under no-till.
risks: Heavy residue can slow spring warming and complicate planting.
Removing stover for feed or sale removes this protection.
gaps: 'Low green cover' is not 'bare soil': NDVI cannot see dead residue, so the field may already be well covered.
Your tillage and residue history are unknown.
actions.expert_check: Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Greenness is low and weather doesn't explain it: scout the field
actions.why_template: {label}, while water, soil moisture and heat are near normal. Check for pests, nutrients, hail or irrigation uniformity.

evidence_specs.text: {value}

benefits: Catching a non-weather problem early (pests, nitrogen, a failed sprinkler package) is often fixable in season.
risks: A 250 m MODIS pixel mixes the field edge with neighbours; the drop may be outside your crop.
gaps: NDVI shows greenness, not cause.
MODIS composites are 16 days, so a recent change may not show yet.
actions.expert_check: Walk the low area or ask your crop consultant to scout it. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Water or heat stress is visible from space
actions.why_template: {label}, at the same time as adverse {cause} conditions. See the water and heat actions for what to check.

evidence_specs.text: {value}

benefits: Confirms that the water and heat warnings are already showing in the crop, which helps decide where limited water goes.
risks: A matching weather signal does not prove the cause; pests or nutrients can coincide.
gaps: NDVI shows greenness, not cause.
Regional weather (~50 km) may differ from your field.
actions.expert_check: Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

actions.title: Many low-green-cover months: consider a rotation with winter wheat (and a cover crop only after a water check)
actions.why_template: This field has about {months} low-green-cover months a year. Winter wheat is green from autumn to early summer, when corn and sorghum fields are not.

evidence_specs.text: Months per year with low green cover (MODIS NDVI < 0.3): {value}
Current rotation: {value}

benefits: A living crop over winter and spring protects soil and shifts part of the water use to spring.
risks: Cover crops USE water: in the Great Plains they can reduce water for the next cash crop (T1_WATER_CONUNDRUM).
Wheat after corn has a tight autumn handoff and disease risks (see T3).
gaps: 'Low green cover' is not 'bare soil': residue is invisible to NDVI.
Cover-crop water evidence is mainly dryland, not limited-irrigation Sheridan 6.
actions.expert_check: Run a water check before adding any cover crop. Review with your agronomist or K-State Research and Extension before acting.

rotation_candidates.name: Continuous corn

agronomy.status_meaning: Supported as a comparison baseline, not confirmed as the farmer's existing rotation or preferred choice.

benefits.finding: A credible limited-irrigation baseline with competitive historical whole-sequence economics.
If corn equipment and a buyer already exist, retaining this sequence avoids adding a second crop's operational requirements; this is a conditional inference.

risks.finding: Every year concentrates demand in summer, especially tasseling/pollination and grain fill. Insufficient peak delivery plus stored water can make it unsuitable even when annual volume appears adequate.
Repeated corn requires field-specific rootworm and residue-borne disease review; no automatic pest-control or nitrogen credit applies.

unknowns: Actual existing sequence and baseline irrigation
Soil profile, rooting restrictions, initial water and nutrient tests
Well output, usable operating hours, efficiency and seasonal budget
Hybrid maturity, pest history, buyer terms and costs

gaps_and_calendar_conflicts.finding: Autumn harvest to next spring sowing leaves an overwinter gap; no same-autumn replant requirement. Wet/cold residue-covered seedbeds or delayed harvest still need checking. Exact gap duration is unresolved.

residue_implications.finding: Retained corn stover can protect soil; actual cover, removal, distribution and tillage determine the effect. High residue can complicate spring establishment.

herbicide_carryover.finding: Review the actual product and crop-trait history even when repeating corn; compatibility is unresolved, not presumed.

market_equipment_prerequisites: Corn-compatible planter and harvest equipment or timely custom service
Drying/storage/hauling capacity and an accepting corn buyer
Budget using farm yields and costs rather than assuming the published corn budget fits the water constraint
agronomy.treatment_basis: No-till limited-irrigation experimental baseline; retain T1_ROTATION_2016 and T1_ROTATION_2021 treatment distinctions. Conventional tillage is not an equivalent tested treatment.

rotation_candidates.why_suggested_base: Comparison baseline: the most-tested limited-irrigation sequence in the western Kansas trials.

rotation_candidates.name: Corn–grain sorghum

agronomy.status_meaning: Directly tested two-year sequence worth comparing; no farm-level superiority established.

benefits.finding: Highest economic ranking in the 2012-2017 study under its assumptions; later multi-year data do not show a significant corn-yield advantage over continuous corn.
Sorghum's later establishment offers a different seasonal schedule. Any weed or irrigation advantage requires an actual management plan.

risks.finding: The direct experiment found less soil water at corn planting after sorghum. Drought tolerance must not be scored as stored-water conservation.

Sorghum still has substantial reproductive demand around boot/heading. Both crops occupy summer; phase-split acreage can still have overlapping demand. Stress-delayed maturity may increase frost exposure.
Both crops can suffer charcoal rot. This is not a general disease break; diagnose the actual pest/pathogen before assigning a benefit.

unknowns: Local sorghum buyer, basis, quality requirements and transport cost
Compatible maturity and latest feasible local sowing date
Pest, weed, herbicide and crop-trait histories

gaps_and_calendar_conflicts.finding: Corn harvest to sorghum sowing and sorghum harvest to next corn sowing both span winter. No wheat-style same-autumn turn is required. Late sorghum harvest can compete with other fall work; actual durations remain unresolved.

residue_implications.finding: Both phases retain cereal residue if it is not removed; distribution and planting through residue must be checked. No measured soil-carbon gain is assigned to changing species.

herbicide_carryover.finding: Check both corn-to-sorghum and sorghum-to-corn transitions against actual product records and current labels. Grass-to-grass rotation does not guarantee compatibility.

market_equipment_prerequisites: Corn equipment plus sorghum-compatible seed metering and harvest setup, owned or contracted
Sorghum drying/aeration/storage capacity verified separately from corn
Buyer acceptance and delivered net price for both grains
agronomy.treatment_basis: Direct no-till sprinkler evidence is T1_ROTATION_2021. T1_ROTATION_2020_ARS provides abstract-level historical economics. The 2016 paper's longer sorghum-containing rotations are not substitutes for this sequence.

rotation_candidates.why_suggested_base: Sorghum is planted later (mid-May to June) and was the top economic ranking in the 2012–2017 study under its assumptions.

rotation_candidates.name: Corn–winter wheat

agronomy.status_meaning: Experimentally demonstrated, but the fall handoff, establishment water and wheat health can prevent suitability.

benefits.finding: Corn following wheat outyielded continuous corn in the later multi-year trial; this alone does not establish whole-sequence profit.

Wheat shifts reproductive demand into spring before corn's summer peak. Fall establishment may also need water. Concurrent phase-split acreage could spread demand; an entire field alternating years does not split demand within a corn year.

risks.finding: Corn harvest can miss timely wheat sowing; little recharge time exists immediately after corn. This is a concrete reason the sequence may be unsuitable.

Corn/volunteer wheat can sustain wheat curl mites; the trial recorded a wheat streak mosaic crop failure. Fusarium head blight after corn is another screening concern, with an explicit eastern-Kansas evidence mismatch.
Historical wheat-phase returns reduced whole-sequence performance in both research periods; do not rank this first from its corn-phase yield.

unknowns: Corn harvest date, grain moisture, drying option and immediate drill availability
Locally acceptable wheat planting window and establishment water
Volunteer wheat and surrounding-host status, disease history and suitable cultivar
Wheat buyer/grade requirements, harvest service and costs
Whether irrigation allocation accounting permits the proposed crop-year timing

gaps_and_calendar_conflicts.finding: Corn year-1 harvest to wheat year-1 sowing is a short or conflicting autumn handoff. Wheat year-2 harvest to corn year-3 sowing leaves summer, autumn and winter for residue-covered recharge, with weed/volunteer management. No second summer crop is inserted.

residue_implications.finding: Wheat stubble can cover the long pre-corn gap. Corn residue preceding wheat creates drill-placement and nitrogen-immobilization concerns; these require local assessment, not a nitrogen credit.

herbicide_carryover.finding: Review corn-to-wheat plant-back compatibility before committing to the short fall turnaround, and wheat-to-corn compatibility before the next phase. No product interval has been assumed.

market_equipment_prerequisites: Residue-capable wheat drill or timely custom drilling immediately after corn
Small-grain harvest capability during the early-summer window
Wheat storage/segregation, accepted grade and buyer; corn equipment remains needed
Include any added machinery/service costs and harvest bottlenecks
agronomy.treatment_basis: Both trials used no-till. The older trial shifted water from wheat to corn; the later report describes approximately equal crop-year applications. Neither is proof of suitability on an unknown soil or under different tillage.

rotation_candidates.why_suggested_base: Wheat uses water in spring and frees the summer; corn after wheat outyielded continuous corn in the later trial.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Field inputs are missing or differ materially from the experiment.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Retain suitability as unknown and regional evidence as provisional. No boundary is needed to display candidates; evidence_status is not field approval.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: A plan fits its seasonal volume but crop-stage supply adequacy has not been checked.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Evaluate peak delivery separately. Stored water and effective rainfall also supply crop demand; a low flow rate is not equivalent to a small annual allocation.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Crop ET ranges or crop labels are being used to calculate pumping savings.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Use a consistent water balance and gross/net definitions. ET differences alone do not determine withdrawal changes; no pumping saving is assigned here.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Comparing treatment results or applying a rotation yield uplift.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Keep the older unequal crop-phase irrigation and later equal-depth trial separate. Neither supplies a universal uplift; annual reports from the same trial are not independent replications.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Corn harvest and field preparation leave uncertain time or water for wheat establishment.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Assess the same-autumn transition; statewide harvest ranges are not proof that a local wheat window remains open.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: The earliest feasible sowing date is later than the locally validated feasible window, with no acceptable operational adjustment.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Exclude that scheduled instance, not the crop everywhere. No universal latest date is invented.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: A two-year sequence is represented as a single annual crop mixture or wheat is sown in its harvest year.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Preserve chronology and both phases. A whole field alternating years and concurrent phase-split acreage impose different annual pumping schedules; confirm applicable allocation accounting separately.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: A next crop is proposed without verified plant-back compatibility.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Keep compatibility unresolved until the actual label and field history are checked. No chemical directions, product-specific interval or inferred restriction is supplied.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: An actual applicable plant-back requirement is verified to conflict with the proposed crop/date.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Exclude the conflicting schedule only after verification; missing history alone triggers a flag.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Species switching is being treated as a crop-family break, disease reduction or nitrogen benefit.
agronomy_rules.rationale: All three crops are grasses. Require outcome-specific evidence; shared hosts and residue immobilization prevent automatic credits.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Corn-wheat is proposed without assessment of green-bridge or residue-associated disease risks.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Review wheat streak mosaic and Fusarium risks separately. The former has direct western Kansas trial relevance; the latter's cited management evidence includes eastern Kansas. Use current regional guidance, not an invented cutoff.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: A sequence is awarded a soil benefit or its intercrop gap is assumed to restore all soil water.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Retained residue, live plant water use and rainfall storage are different processes. Assess establishment and recharge; do not add a living cover crop or carbon gain by default.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Any required market or operational capability is unverified.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Adding sorghum or wheat is conditional on executable production and marketing. Include added costs; do not presume corn facilities fit every grain.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Numerical yield, profit or pumping comparisons are requested without these inputs and a validated model implementation.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Return qualitative comparison and unresolved numerical outputs. Trial averages and budget scenarios are not response functions. Do not fit a monotonic yield curve from observational water-use associations.

agronomy_rules.condition_description: Ranking from corn-phase yield alone, mixing budget versions, or comparing different return definitions.
agronomy_rules.rationale: Compare the complete cycle on the same area-time and cost basis. Label the retrieved 2026 budgets and their 2025 publication date; replace assumptions with farm inputs.
